name: Aaron Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and a junior operator on a cable-winding machine. Secondary school was as far as I went, and I spent years in dispatch before moving to the winding room. I watch the spool edge and stop the feed when a loop bunches; the technician still checks my tension settings. A neat spool is satisfying to lift off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife stocks shelves at a pharmacy, and our grown children live on their own. The weekend premium puts my machine pay above the usual rate, and we have about eleven months of expenses saved. There are several cable and packaging plants within a bus ride, so similar work is plentiful. I use AI now and then to sort a shopping list or explain a word, but only after a person shows me it works. We would like me to stop at 67 in 2035 if actual income after work covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that no chatbot untangles a cable loop on a moving spool. We need a technician to teach the safe stop, and a junior has to watch the first metres closely. A company that keeps good operators deserves repeat orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend rate and our savings leave us comfortable. I am still learning the winder, so I don't assume every good spool is my doing. If the job carries on, I have time to get more accurate and see whether stopping at 67 really adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first spool of each new cable size with the technician. I'll log any loops I stop and put some fresh weekend pay into our reserve after regular bills. At home my wife and I will update our food and rent figures before talking about leaving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. We can handle a broken spool without treating the whole future as broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a cable loop unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cable starts to cross itself near the rim. I stop the feed, mark the length and ask the technician to check tension before another spool is wound. Pulling at the loop while the drum turns would be foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes your current money steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our eleven-month reserve came from paid weekends and my wife's steady pharmacy hours. We still need ongoing income after I stop, and I won't guess at it. The reserve gives us time to ask the right questions.

say: A **crossed cable loop** still needs a safe stop and a technician.
Good operators and **reliable spools** help the plant keep customers.
think: Our **weekend premium** and eleven-month reserve make present bills secure.
I am still **junior at winding** and cannot assume a good run proves mastery.
do: **Check** first spools with the technician and log stopped loops.
**Save** fresh weekend wages after bills while updating household costs.
S0.quote: We can handle a broken spool without treating the whole future as broken.
fieldNote: His **higher weekend pay**, regular partner income and eleven-month reserve support present security despite junior machine skill.
The **new deposits** come from weekend wages; the household cost list is preparation for a conditional retirement decision.

steps.text: Check first cable spool with technician after size changes
Save new weekend wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may plan cable orders before robots can wind and carry spools safely. If the technician has tested a display that spots bad tension, I will learn it. I will not let a screen replace the guard or the person who knows the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software might shorten batches and take a weekend from my rota. Our reserve and nearby plants mean we have options, but I would rather keep the premium while I can. I use AI occasionally at home, yet that does not qualify me to set a cable winder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the technician to show me the plant's approved tension display on a paid shift after it has been tested, and compare it with the physical first spool. I'll compare the posted weekend rota and premium with four pay slips. If a paid guarded coil-check course is offered, I'll enrol and practise the safe stop with the technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible weekend cut, but I have time to check a real rota. A predicted bad spool is useful only if the cable is checked before it goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you learn the approved tension display?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn which colour on the display means a high-tension run, then look at the actual winding edge. The technician should show me a known bad spool first. I would use the screen as a warning, not as permission to reach into a turning drum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a weekend cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posted weekend shifts and premium line have to match the pay slips. If either falls, I would ask the supervisor for the number and reason. I won't choose a new job over a rumour about a computer.

say: **Order AI** may change batches before robots handle cable spools.
I will learn a **tested tension display** beside the technician and the real machine.
think: A shorter batch could remove **weekend premium** pay.
Our **reserve and local jobs** give options, but a new plant may pay less.
do: **Learn** the approved tested tension display with the technician on paid time.
**Compare** weekend rota with pay slips and attend a paid guarded coil course if offered.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible premium cut, with options to respond.
S1.quote: A predicted bad spool is useful only if the cable is checked before it goes out.
fieldNote: His **occasional home AI use** differs from learning a tested approved plant display with hands-on verification.
A **coil course** requires an offered paid guarded place, while a premium complaint depends on actual rota and pay slips.

steps.text: Learn approved tested tension display with technician on paid shift
Compare posted weekend rota and premium with four pay slips
Enrol in coil-check course if paid guarded practical place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife that thinking AI could handle cable orders by 2028 and capable robots might wind and move spools about 2031, when I am 63. I would ask the plant what happens to the weekend rota. We can look elsewhere, but only at jobs that really exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose most of the premium if robots run the winding room. Eleven months saved gives us room, and several local plants give choices, but we still need a wage until retirement is affordable. I would not stop at 63 just because a machine arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for written staffing and paid-hour plans. If the plant offers a funded paid guarded coil-inspection place, I'll enrol and pass its practical test. If the winding shifts fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing roles only if net pay after travel covers our bills; after qualifying, I'll apply to posted cable-inspection roles on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a big loss of weekend pay, though we have saved enough to search carefully. A full cupboard is not the same as a wage next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would cable-inspection training test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician should put a damaged coil in front of me and watch me mark its bad length, stop the guarded drum and reject the spool. Those practice hours must be paid and the course fee covered. Our savings should stay available for living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge another factory job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting needs the base wage, paid shift length and site. We would subtract the journey and compare the rest with rent and food. I would not take a poorly guarded night job just because another factory calls it winding.

say: **2031 robots** might wind spools when I am 63.
The plant should give **written paid-hour plans** before changing the weekend rota.
think: Most **weekend premium** pay could go before retirement is affordable.
Our **eleven-month reserve** and nearby plants provide choices, not permanent income.
do: **Request** written hours and attend funded paid guarded coil inspection if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local packing or qualified cable inspection if shifts fall and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about major possible premium loss, with money and jobs to navigate it.
S2.quote: A full cupboard is not the same as a wage next month.
fieldNote: He sees a **possible large premium loss** but has a year of savings and multiple nearby plants.
The **inspection path** needs funded paid guarded training and qualification; both searches need posted safe local work at viable net pay.

steps.text: Enrol in coil inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if shifts fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local cable inspection if qualified, shifts fall, net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan orders in 2031 and robots might handle cable drums around 2034, when I am 66. That is a year before my hoped-for stop. I would rather count the money than argue that every machine must fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may need one more year of the weekend wage before 67. If our documented income after work will cover the bills in 2035, I can stop then. If not, we will use our reserve for breathing room while I seek a safe paid role, not pretend it is a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I will compare written income available after work with our monthly costs. If the figures cover the bills at 67, I'll stop the cable shift in 2035. If I am still working when robots arrive in 2034 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local winding or packing roles only if net pay after travel is enough; I'll ask the technician to sign off a safe coil check if a posted role requires that qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the last paid year I may need, though there are other plants. A lost weekend cable shift costs more when retirement is a year away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures decide whether 2035 works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly income after my wage ends, not a guessed entitlement. My wife's pharmacy hours and our food and rent costs go beside it. If the page falls short, I keep working in a safe paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a later winding job offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only to a real posting with safe guards, paid hours and a base wage that survives the bus fare. A coil-check role would need a practical qualification, not merely my request for a sign-off. If the course is required, I would enrol only with a funded paid guarded place.

say: **2031 planning AI** comes before robots handle spools around 2034.
I hope to stop at **67**, provided documented income covers household costs.
think: I might need the **2034 weekend wage** for one more year.
The **strong reserve** buys time to search, not income for life.
do: **Check** written post-work income and stop in 2035 only if bills are covered.
**Apply** to posted safe local winding or packing if still employed, hours fall and net pay works.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible lost final paid year.
S3.quote: A lost weekend cable shift costs more when retirement is a year away.
fieldNote: His **2035 stop** is conditional on documented income, while robot arrival in 2034 could threaten a needed final year.
Any **later application** needs continued employment, lost hours and a posted safe local role at adequate net pay; specialist work adds qualification.

steps.text: Compare written post-work income with household rent and food
Stop cable shift at 67 in 2035 if documented income covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may arrange cable orders in 2036, when I am 68, and able robots could wind drums around 2039, when I am 71. I hope to have stopped in 2035. Even a tested machine will not decide what my household can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our eleven months saved and good weekend wage make a decent start, but they do not promise income after I leave. If verified figures let me stop at 67, I will. If the figures fail, I may still be winding cable when order AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my wife and I will put documented post-work income beside rent, food and other costs. I'll keep paid weekend shifts while we check. If the figures cover bills, I'll stop in 2035 at 67; if I am still employed after 2036 and shifts fall, I'll apply to posted safe local cable work only where net pay after travel still covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about an unverified income figure, though the longer warning gives us room. I will not trade a real weekend wage for a date circled on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence supports a 2035 stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need an actual monthly amount that would arrive after my wages end. We would compare it with rent, food and transport, without assuming a pension or my wife's hours are guaranteed forever. If it does not cover costs, I keep the wage while it is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local posting needs a safe winder, paid hours and a base wage that works after the bus ride. I would only apply if I were still working and had lost shifts after 2036. If I have already stopped with enough income, the application stays unsent.

A **2035 retirement** happens only if actual post-work money pays the bills.

If the figures fail, I may still be **working after 2036**.

S4.quote: I will not trade a real weekend wage for a date circled on the fridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 one. Robots might cut the weekend cable shifts at 63 before we know if we can afford to stop at 67. Written staffing hours, a funded paid guarded coil course and real safe local postings with enough net pay would help. Our savings give us time, not a second wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the cable after the first spool is wound. One crossed cable loop can hide under a clean outer layer.

headlineQuote: One crossed cable loop can hide under a clean outer layer.
portrait: **Aaron**, 58, is a junior cable-winding operator with secondary schooling and occasional checked AI use.
He and his pharmacy-stockworker wife have **grown children**, higher weekend pay, eleven months saved and many nearby plants.
His **traditional outlook** favours work and family responsibility, while his steady adaptability trusts tools after a technician tests them.
He is **anxious** about a fast premium loss; stopping at 67 depends on documented post-work income covering bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring spool-handling robots by 2031 and cut weekend pay before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing hours**, funded paid guarded coil training and real safe local roles with enough net pay would help.
